newsitem.title: USA: Forecasts for Fed ease gather momentum -- US experts.
newsitem.headline: Forecasts for Fed ease gather momentum -- US experts.

text.p: A long-awaited tightening of credit policy by the Federal Reserve might not come in 1996.
In fact, it may not come at all, according to a growing group of economists, predicting the central bank's next monetary policy adjustment will be an easing of credit.
But an easing isn't right around the corner either.
Indeed, any relaxation of credit won't arrive until the latter part of 1997, the economists said.
"I don't think it's going to happen for a while," said Christopher Low, senior economist at HSBC Markets Inc.
"We'll probably have to wait until the end of next year. But the bottom line is that growth has been slowing, and I think that will continue," Low added.

The economy grew at a 2.2-percent pace in the third quarter, according to a Commerce Department preliminary estimate. That is down from a 4.7-percent rate in the second quarter, and a 2.0-percent pace from January to March.

Low said his firm expects a 2.0-percent pace of growth in the final quarter of this year, followed by a slightly stronger rate of 2.5-percent early next year, and then growth of less than 2.0 percent for the rest of 1997.
But slackening growth is only half the story, experts said. That, combined with a declining Consumer Price Index (CPI), will at a minimum force the Fed to stand pat.
"We see CPI inflation coming down all year next year," said Low. "That's the icing on the cake that will allow Fed policymakers to go ahead and cut rates."
Michelle Colley Laughlin, Treasury market strategist at Prudential Securities Inc, agreed the central bank's next policy move would be an easing in the fourth quarter of 1997.
Laughlin and other experts pointed to the latest survey from Alexandria, Va.-based Blue Chip Financial Forecasts.
Blue Chip's November newsletter posed a special question on Fed policy to which 41 economists responded.
Sixty-three percent said the Fed's next move would be a tightening of credit, while 37 percent expected an easing, according to Randy Moore, executive editor at Blue Chip.
The group calling for a tightening shrunk from 80 percent a month ago and 90 percent in August. The easing camp swelled to its current 37 percent from 10 percent in August.
When Blue Chip first introduced a Fed policy question in late March, Moore said the survey showed 83 percent in the easing contingent and 17 percent in the tightening one.
"You can see the tide has been shifting," Laughlin said.
"The third quarter did show the slowdown (Fed Chairman Alan) Greenspan was looking for. It was enough to even the odds about the direction of the next Fed move," she added.
Reuters last Friday surveyed Wall Street economists about the near-term direction of Fed policy.
Less than a handful of the 21 pundits polled said they expect the Fed to next relax credit, with the bulk of experts predicting the central bank to remain on hold.
Still, a poll done on the same day by Boston-based Technical Data Inc yielded different results.

The financial advisory firm said 89 percent of experts surveyed forecast the Fed's next 25-basis-point move would come in early 1997. Fifty-six percent said the move would be a tightening, while 33 percent said it would be an ease.
"I'm with them 100 percent on the early '97," said Nancy Kimmelman, chief economist at Technical Data. "But whether it's a tightening or an ease, I don't know."
Kimmelman said she, and probably most economists, had been operating under the assumption that the risk of inflation in the economy was higher than it was now proving to be.
As a result she said, "The Fed can probably hang out longer than originally thought."
-- N.A. Treasury Desk, 212-859-1661
